group_assessment.weighting: The Siena neonatal biochemistry group (Buonocore, Perrone), long-standing authors on oxidative stress in newborns; the review is a secondary summary of trials and animal studies, with no new data, and concerns preterm infants. Weighted as a map of saturation-target trials, not as evidence for any disease.

queries.query: WWOX AND (hyperoxia OR hyperbaric OR oxygen therapy)

multihop.note: No WWOX-direct reference. The five saturation-target trials (SUPPORT, BOOST II, COT, STOP-ROP, BOOST I) are named in the text; their primary reports were not opened.

entries.proposition: Genre: a narrative review of oxygen toxicity and saturation targets in newborns, mainly preterm; it has no Methods section, no search description, no figures and no tables. WWOX and genetic encephalopathy are not discussed.
entries.snippet: This review focuses on the mechanisms of ROS production and ROS-induced toxic effects following oxygen administration in newborns

entries.proposition: Population limit: the vulnerability argument rests on preterm antioxidant immaturity and the premature infant is the named at-risk group.
entries.snippet: Therefore, premature infants are especially prone to oxidant injury, being unprepared for hyperoxic challenge of extrauterine life.

entries.proposition: Hyperoxia is linked to injury of lung, retina and red cells, and the retina mechanism involves HIF-1 alpha and VEGF in the developing vessels.
entries.snippet: the developing retinal endothelial cells activate various transcription factors, including HIF-1α and vascular endothelial growth factor

entries.proposition: Long-term: neonatal hyperoxia in mice is linked to adult neurodevelopmental impairment (abnormal behaviour, memory deficits, small hippocampus) without intracranial pathology; this is rodent evidence cited in the review.
entries.snippet: neurodevelopmental impairments in adult life, as demonstrated by abnormal behavior, deficits in spatial and recognition memory, small hippocampal dimensions

entries.proposition: Trial evidence: lowering the saturation target reduced severe retinopathy but raised death before discharge in SUPPORT and death and necrotising enterocolitis in BOOST II.
entries.snippet: the use of a lower range of oxygen saturation results in a decrease of occurrence of severe ROP and an increase of death before the discharge

entries.proposition: BOOST II: restrictive oxygen use below 90 percent saturation raised death and necrotising enterocolitis.
entries.snippet: a restrictive use of oxygen, with target range of saturation below 90%, is associated with a higher risk of death and necrotizing enterocolitis

entries.proposition: The review's own advice is not unitary: abstract and text give an alarm range of 90 to 95 percent, one cited centre used below 85 and above 93 percent, and the final paragraph proposes alarms at 91 and 96 percent.
entries.snippet: it has been suggested to set the acoustic signals at 91 and 96%, with a delay time not longer than 20 s

entries.proposition: The consensus statement: guidelines suggest a target of 90 to 95 percent for infants below 28 weeks of gestation up to 36 weeks postmenstrual age.
entries.snippet: the 2013 European Consensus Guidelines on the Management of Neonatal Respiratory Distress Syndrome in Preterm Infants suggested that SpO2 should be targeted at 90–95%

entries.proposition: The review concedes the optimum remains unknown and that pulse oximetry accuracy is itself controversial.
entries.snippet: the optimal target range for oxygen saturation in the sick newborns and, above all, in the extremely preterm babies is not clear

entries.proposition: Its bottom line is to avoid both hypoxia and hyperoxia in infants needing oxygen, with no antioxidant intervention endorsed.
entries.snippet: the most careful approach is to avoid both hypoxia and hyperoxia in infants requiring oxygen supplementation
